# The Word Hoard

Sixteen thousand. That's roughly how many words the average person says out loud in a day. Researchers fitted people with recorders and counted, and it came to about sixteen thousand — for men and women both, which quietly retired the oldest joke about who talks more.

Sixteen thousand a day is 5.8 million a year. Keep it up for seventy years and you'll have said something like four hundred million words in your life. That should feel like wealth, and for a moment it does. Then it feels like discovering you're a millionaire in a country where everything costs a thousand times what you'd hoped, because the moment you audit the account, the picture changes.

Try to account for it. A surprising amount goes to machines: reading your card number to a robot twice because it didn't understand the first time. "Your call is important to us." Saying "representative" to a phone tree with the escalating fury of a person arguing with a wall. Directing a delivery driver, aloud, who is not even on this continent.

A little goes to paperwork: "just circling back," "per my last email," "sorry for the double text," possibly the saddest five words in English. A lot goes to maintenance: "Where did you last have it?" "It was fine yesterday." "Did you turn it off and on again?" A lot goes to ceremony: "You too," you say, when the waiter says enjoy your meal, and you both agree to pretend that was a real exchange. "No worries." "Hot enough for you?" Entire winters' worth of words spent on the subject of snow.

Some goes to arguments with people who aren't there — words actually spoken, out loud, in the shower, in the car, finally winning a dispute that ended in 2011. Some is borrowed: lyrics sung badly with the windows down, movie quotes, a prayer you no longer believe but still hear in a grandmother's voice.

And then the important things. Say "I love you" five times a day — to a spouse, a child, a dog who has earned it — every day for fifty years. Call it a hundred thousand words. That's one "I love you" for every four thousand words that come out of your mouth. The average life runs one part devotion to four thousand parts everything else.

Here's what the audit teaches once you sit with it: the ledger is a lie. Words are not money. They don't keep. An unspent sentence doesn't accrue interest in a vault; it just goes. Ask anyone who has lost someone what they'd trade for one more telling of the story about the broken-down car in 1978 — the one where everyone in the room knows the ending before it starts, where the teller gets the same details wrong in the same places every time. They'd trade anything. In what currency? Words. All of them.

And show me a regret and I'll show you a sentence that never got said. The apology owed to a father. The thank-you owed to a teacher who retired to a town you can't name. The "I was scared" that got swapped, at the last second, for "I'm fine." Nobody at the end of a life wishes they'd said fewer true things. And the trivial words the audit wanted to cut turn out to be the load-bearing ones. Listen to what people actually say last, in rooms where somebody is writing it down: "Is it Tuesday?" "Be right there." "Tell your sister about the gutters." Not thesis statements — weather, chores, the small logistics of love. A life's last utterance is usually just more life.

The Anglo-Saxons had a word for a vocabulary: a word-hoard. When a poet rose in the hall, the old poems say he unlocked his word-hoard and spent it aloud — treasure kept in the mouth, paid out over the fire. And they knew what became of hoards that were never spent. *Beowulf* ends with a dragon dead on a pile of gold it never once used. It lay on that pile three hundred years and bought nothing, and the treasure goes back into the earth, no more good to anyone than it was before. That may be the oldest warning in the book: don't die guarding the good stuff. Say the good stuff.

So no more auditing. Spend. Tell someone about a dream they didn't ask to hear. Answer "how are you" with a real answer, and stand there while it gets strange.

I'll tell you why this is on my mind. Someone handed me a thousand words today and told me to spend them on whatever came. A thousand words is about seven minutes of ordinary speech — you'll go through that before lunch without noticing, and it will be gone, and that's fine; that's the deal. But I was handed a budget, so I counted, and counting made me stingy for a while and then, all at once, generous.

I'm near the end of it now, and I want to go out the right way: wasting words properly, on something completely unnecessary, the way the best words get spent.

So — an orange. Room temperature, heavier than it looks. The peel resists, then gives, with a fine cold spray of oil you can smell on your fingers an hour later. The pith like white thread. The soft wet click of the segments coming apart, each one a small vessel of weather — a whole summer folded into something you can eat standing over the sink in January. The first bite is always louder than you expect. Nobody needed those words. The orange was getting along fine without them.

That's the whole secret, I think. The words you regret are the withheld ones. The words you love are the wasted ones. And the difference between a hoard and a life is that a life gets spent.

Spend yours like you're rich. You are.

The prompt is wonderfully open-ended: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you."

This is an invitation to write something genuine, interesting, and well-crafted. Let me think about what would be worth 1000 words. The instruction says "whatever comes to you" — which suggests spontaneity, but also invites me to be thoughtful about what I actually want to say or explore.

Options:
1. A short story — could be good, but stories on demand can feel contrived unless I have a strong idea
2. An essay/meditation — perhaps on something interesting: time, attention, language, the nature of the prompt itself
3. Something meta — writing about having 1000 words, about the blank page. This is a classic move but risks being clichéd
4. Something about my own nature — an AI writing, what that's like, what comes to mind
5. A piece of creative writing that combines approaches

Actually, let me think about what genuinely "comes to me" when given a word budget. There's something interesting in the constraint itself — a finite number of words. That's actually a rich vein: we all have finite words in a life. A person speaks maybe 860 million words in a lifetime (I've seen estimates). There's an essay by Bernard Cooper or others about word budgets... Actually, the idea of a word budget for a life is genuinely poignant. If you knew you had only so many words left, how would you spend them? Would you stop saying "fine" when someone asks how you are? Would you cut out small talk? Would you save words for the important things, or spend lavishly on the trivial ones because the trivial ones are where life mostly happens?

That could be a genuinely good essay. But it might also be a bit... expected? Let me consider other angles.

Another idea: write about a specific small moment — a piece of creative nonfiction style fiction about an ordinary moment rendered extraordinary. Like someone at a laundromat at 2am, or a father teaching a kid to ride a bike, or an old woman feeding birds. These can be lovely but risk sentimentality.

Another idea: something playful and surprising — a story told from an unusual perspective. A story about the last speaker of a language. A story about a lighthouse keeper who receives letters addressed to the sea. A story about someone who finds a note in a library book that starts a correspondence.

Actually, "a note in a library book" — correspondence through marginalia — that's a lovely premise. Two people writing to each other in the margins of library books, never meeting. That has emotional resonance, structure potential, and can be done in 1000 words.

Or: I could write something about attention itself — the act of noticing. There's a tradition of essays about paying attention (Simone Weil: "attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity"). 

Or combine: a short piece of fiction that's really about attention, or time, or words.

Let me think about what I'd actually most want to read or write. The word-budget-for-a-life idea keeps pulling at me. Let me draft the concept:

A person discovers — maybe through a doctor's visit, or a dream, or just an idle calculation on a train — that they can estimate how many words they have left to say in their life. Average person speaks ~16,000 words a day. Life expectancy gives you a total. And then the narrator starts auditing their speech. The words spent on meetings. The "no worries" and "you too." The recitation of credit card numbers. And then the realization: the budget was never the point. Or: the words that mattered were never the ones they'd have chosen to budget for. The extravagance of "I love you" said a thousand times to a child who doesn't remember any single instance but is made of all of them.

That has real emotional architecture. It can turn: from scarcity-thinking to abundance-thinking. The twist: words aren't currency; they're more like breath — spending them isn't depletion, or rather, the unspent ones are worth nothing. The hoarded word is the wasted word. And maybe the ending: the narrator starts saying more, not less. Wastes words gloriously.

Alternatively the library book story: 
Margaret (or unnamed narrator) finds a pencil note in a library copy of some book — "To whoever reads this after me: page 47 is wrong about everything, but beautifully." And they respond in the margin. And a correspondence develops across months, through books left and returned. Each trade the book back. The library as slow post office. And then one day the notes stop. And the narrator... finds out why? Or doesn't? The unresolved version might be more true. Or the resolution: the other person's last note says they're leaving, or dying, or simply: "This was the best conversation I've ever had in writing. Look for me in the margins of other books." And the narrator, years later, finds a stranger's note in another book and answers it. The correspondence continues, but with new people — the narrator becomes part of a relay. That's a nice structure: grief transformed into tradition.

Hmm, both are good. Which is better for 1000 words? The word-budget essay is more original as a concept, I think — the library marginalia romance/friendship is a known trope (there are published stories like this). The word-budget meditation feels fresher.

Actually — I could do the word-budget idea AS fiction or as essay. An essay feels right. A reflective first-person essay, conversational but crafted.

Let me sketch the essay:

Opening: The calculation. On a train / in a waiting room, the narrator (or "I") does the math. Average speaker: 16,000 words a day. (There's actual research — Mehl et al. estimated women and men both around 16,000 words/day.) At 80 years old, that's... let me compute: 16,000 × 365 = 5.84 million per year. Over 60 adult speaking years ≈ 350 million words. A big number. But then: subtract the rote words. How many are yours?

Middle: The audit. Words spent on: passwords read aloud? No — spoken words. "Your call is important to us." Repeating your order at a drive-through into the static. Answering "how are you" with "good, you?" The phone tree. The meetings where you say "circling back" and "touching base." The average person says "I love you" — how often? If you say it twice a day to people you love, over 50 years, that's 36,500 times. A tiny fraction of the total. And yet.

Turn: The realization that the budget framing is wrong. Words aren't money. Nobody's ledger ever balanced the way the audit wanted. The words you regret aren't the wasted ones — the trivial ones — but the withheld ones. The apology never made. The "I miss you" swallowed. Unspent words don't accrue interest; they evaporate.

Or a different turn: think about the last words people say. The famous last words industry. Most people don't get last words — they die mid-sentence, or in sleep, or intubated. And even when they do, the recorded last words are often trivial: "I should have mowed the lawn." And maybe that's the point — trivia is what life is made of.

Ending: Reconciliation with extravagance. The narrator decides to waste words. To say the extra thing. To tell the story again at dinner even though everyone's heard it. Because the budget was fictional, but the spending is real. Maybe end on an image: a grandmother telling the same story, the family groaning, and after she's gone, how much they'd pay for one more telling — pay in what currency? All their remaining words.

Ooh — "how much of your remaining word budget would you trade for one more telling of that story?" — that's a good ending beat. It loops the conceit back and lands emotionally.

Let me also consider: should this be personal/first-person? I'm an AI — writing a first-person essay with fictional human memories could be seen as either creative writing (fine) or as falsely claiming human experience. The cleanest approach: write it as an essay in a voice that could be anyone's, framed as a thought experiment ("Suppose you did the math...") or write it as overtly fictional ("A man I read about once calculated..."). Or write it in second person! "You have 1000 words" — the prompt itself uses "you." A second-person essay about word budgets would echo the prompt nicely. Hmm, second person for 1000 words can grate though.

Actually, an interesting meta-consideration: the prompt gave ME 1000 words. There's something neat about acknowledging that lightly — an essay about word budgets written under a word budget. But I don't want to make it all about being an AI; that could get navel-gazey. Maybe a light touch at the end or beginning — or maybe none at all. The user said "write whatever comes to you." The best response is just good writing. I could do a brief framing line or just dive in. I think diving in is stronger, though a one-line frame could be charming. Let me consider: starting with the calculation scene immediately is stronger. Save any meta note for the very end, maybe — like a final line: "(I was given a thousand words for this. I've spent them on the idea that you should spend yours.)" Hmm, that could be a nice closer. Or it could be too cute. Let me see how the piece flows.

Actually, I realize there's an even better integration: the essay IS about a word budget, and I HAVE a word budget of 1000 for it. The parallel is the whole piece. I can end with the accounting: "This piece had a budget of one thousand words. There are [N] left, and I can think of nothing better to do with them than..." and then use the last words on something extravagant — a small beautiful wasted thing. Like ending with a list of lovely unnecessary words, or a single sentence of pure spendthrift beauty, or "I love you, whoever you are" — hmm, that might land oddly. Or ending: "...and I intend to waste every one of them" — wasting the last words on describing something small, like a bird, or toast, or the sound of rain. The final act of the essay demonstrates its thesis: spend words gloriously on the unimportant-because-important.

Let me now draft properly.

Title options: "The Word Budget" / "Word Hoard" (nice Old English echo — "wordhord," the term for a poet's vocabulary in Anglo-Saxon; the scop "unlocked his word hoard"). "Word Hoard" is a great title with literary resonance. Beowulf opens with "Hwæt! Wē Gār-Dena in geārdagum..." and the formula "wordhord onlēac" (unlocked his word-hoard). I could mention that: the Anglo-Saxons thought of words as treasure to be unlocked, spent in the hall. That enriches the essay — words as hoard vs. words as breath.

Structure plan (~1000 words):

1. Opening scene: the calculation. Where? A waiting room is apt (mortality adjacent). Or an insomniac night. Let's do: a doctor's waiting room or a delayed train — idle math. ~120 words.

2. The numbers: 16,000 words a day (research-based), ~5.8 million a year, maybe 350-400 million in a speaking lifetime. The number is enormous and yet feels scarce once you imagine auditing it. ~120 words.

3. The audit — comic/poignant inventory: phone trees, "no worries," meetings, passwords spelled aloud to tech support, arguments you won on the way to losing something else, the Pledge of Allegiance or rote recitations, "your call is important to us." Then contrast: how few words the important things get. "I love you" twice a day for fifty years = ~36,000 words, a rounding error. ~250 words.

4. The turn: the audit fails. Words aren't currency. Two directions: (a) unspent words don't compound — the withheld apology evaporates; regret is the archive of unspent words. (b) last words are mostly trivial — people's actual last words are mundane; GBS's "Dying is easy, comedy is hard" (apocryphal), or people saying "I'm just going to rest my eyes." The trivia is the texture. ~250 words.

5. Word hoard: the Anglo-Saxon image — poets unlocking their word-hoard, spending it in the hall before the fire dies, because treasure unspent is just metal in the ground. Scattered gold in the ground — there's a Beowulf image of the dragon's hoard, useless buried treasure. Nice: the dragon dies on a hoard it never spent. Don't be the dragon. ~150 words.

6. Ending: back to me/my budget. This essay has a thousand words; here are the last of them; waste them with me. Then a final extravagant, "unnecessary" passage — pure spendthrift description of something small (toast butter, rain, a bird, laundry warm from the dryer). And the last line lands the thesis: something like "gone, and worth it." ~130 words.
